extracted.intended_audience: scholars and students of medieval/ancient natural history and botany; translators of Latin scientific texts
extracted.subtask_description: A fragment of a medieval/ancient natural-history treatise (De Plantis / De Animalibus) discussing plant parts, temperaments, propagation, preservation, pigments, and theories of animal generation. Useful for translation, annotation, and historical interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mapping plant parts to temperaments
rubrics_metrics.description: Partium plantarum temperamentum — assignment of typical qualities (hot/cold, dry/moist) to plant parts (leaves, root, flower, fruit, cortex/bark, pith/matrix, wood).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text enumerates which plant parts are typically most dry/hot or most moist/cold and explains functional consequences: e.g., leaves, flowers, fruits, seed, bark, wood, pith each have characteristic temperaments affecting nutrition and use. This mapping is used to predict behavior (e.g., which parts produce tears/latex, which preserve or rot) and to guide uses (medicinal, culinary, preservative).

rubrics_metrics.name: Leaf-number and apex imparity rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Folia in summitate plantarum imparia sunt — leaves at the apex of a plant tend to be odd-numbered (imparia) due to the pattern of nerves and node development.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author argues that a central (median) leaf at the apex is larger/stronger and that typical phyllotaxy (pairs at nodes, with a median added at the top) explains why terminal leaf arrangements are odd. Use presence/absence and relative size of the median leaf as an indicator of normal development and as a taxonomic clue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leaflet count reflects material thickness and vascular structure
rubrics_metrics.description: The number of leaflets (enophyllum, trifolium, pentaphyllon, heptaphyllon, etc.) correlates with the thickness of the plant material and the number of nerves: more leaflets imply more nerves and a sturdier structure; fewer leaflets correlate with thinner material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing or classifying a plant, note leaflet number to infer internal structure and vigor; very thin plants tend to have few leaflets and fewer nerves, while trees have many nerves and leaflets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing of leaf vs flower emergence predicts fruit fate
rubrics_metrics.description: If leaves emerge before flowers, fruits are prone to perish (e.g., in winter); if leaves appear after or at the same time, fruits are likelier to mature and persist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use phenology (sequence of leaf and flower emergence) as a predictive diagnostic: plants whose leaves develop earlier than flowers often have fruits that fail by winter, while those with leaves that persist or appear at appropriate times better protect/complete fruit maturation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fruit humidity, ripening frequency, and quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Fruits that ripen multiple times per year (e.g., fig, vine, sycamore) are very moist/fat and thus more nutritious but hard to mature evenly; fruits that ripen once and quickly are drier and more readily preserved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess fruit preservation and culinary/seed quality by their ripening pattern and moisture: repeatedly-fruiting trees produce humid, rich fruits that may not fully mature without care; single-ripening, dry fruits tend to be less prone to putrefaction and have different uses (e.g., storage, seed viability).

rubrics_metrics.name: Seed robustness linked to fruit pulp and exposure
rubrics_metrics.description: Seeds contained in fruits with aqueous (watery) pulp become more robust and better suited for generation; pedicel attachment and fruit exposure to air influence seed development.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging seed quality for propagation, prefer seeds from fruits with abundant aqueous nutritive pulp and from fruits that matured without excessive pedicel suspension; these seeds are described as stronger and more apt to generate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transplanting and propagation methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical criteria for moving plants between regions: transplant female (or fruit-bearing) specimens in intact vessels and soil for tender germlings; use cuttings buried in moist, temperate, sweet, non-rancid earth to enable rooting and survival.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text advises which parts to transport, how to pack them (intact soil/vessels vs buried cuttings), and the preferred soil moisture/temperature (slightly moist, sweet, tempered) for successful transplant, noting that some operations (mass grafting/large experiments) are long, risky and often futile.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preservation of harvested produce and tubers
rubrics_metrics.description: Methods to prevent putrefaction: drying, refrigerating, burying in moist earth, long cooking and storage in cool places preserve tubers and fruits; putrefaction arises from aqueous humidity and heat.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different preservation techniques suit different substances: drying or intense heat (threefold fires, smoke) removes moisture; refrigeration/glaciation prevents putrefaction; oily or moist-preserved foods resist rot (e.g., cheeses or fish preserved in oil). Practical recipes: cook tubers long, store in a cool place to avoid rot; bury certain items in damp earth to recover them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selecting and evaluating plant oils
rubrics_metrics.description: Criteria for good oil: abundance and optimal quality in the producing plant; 'optimus simpliciter'—simple, plentiful, sweet oil is best. Specific plants (linseed, heliotrope, nuts, almonds, rape, henna, certain fruit kernels) are recommended sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose oil sources by yield and sensory qualities (color, sweetness). Some oils are household staples or medicinally prized; the author lists regional varieties (e.g., Benin phasellus cortex) and notes differences in aroma, pungency, and uses (unguent, lamp oil, medicinal).

rubrics_metrics.name: Preparation of pigments, inks, and varnishes for books/paints
rubrics_metrics.description: Procedural recipe-style guidance for making red/purple/black pigments and varnishes: e.g., mixing cinnabar with other substances, maceration times (eight days), boiling until one-third of water remains, adding quicklime (calchantum), and using linseed oil varnishes to protect colors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text prescribes exact manipulations and cautions about permanence: thin papers and wet inks fade quickly; using calx-derived concentrates and oil-based varnishes improves durability of pigments on manuscripts and paintings. It also warns that some methods produce ephemeral results and gives techniques for erasure (abrasion, particular powders).

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification by feeding habits, dentition, and armature
rubrics_metrics.description: Animals are classed according to diet (herbivores vs carnivores vs mixed) and corresponding physical equipment: herbivores have hooves and horns, carnivores have teeth and claws; birds differ in beak structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use anatomical features (teeth, claws, hooves, horns) to infer diet and behavior. The text links morphology with function (e.g., in equids, cattle), and notes exceptions and mixed feeders (humans, certain primates).

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria to infer origin of animals (egg/womb vs putrefaction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Diagnostic criteria distinguishing animals generated from putrid matter versus those from eggs/womb: animals from putrid matter are often imperfect, small, weak, less capable of producing similar offspring; those from eggs/womb are more perfect and prudent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author reasons that generative quality depends on the material and enclosure: generation from putrefaction tends to yield weaker, often monstrous forms with impaired faculties; generation from eggs or womb (or other 'certain' materials like bee-male) yields more perfect animals. Use vigor, size, and capacity to reproduce as indicators of origin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental caution for grafting/transferring cultivars
rubrics_metrics.description: Large-scale experimentation on many trees (mass grafting, moving many plants) is risky, time-consuming, and often unproductive; failures are frequent and yield little useful result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text counsels prudence: avoid broad, repetitive trials without careful planning; first successful innovators in a locale often receive blame yet practical reward accrues to implementers; prefer measured, local experiments and expect long intervals before results.
